lead: Real op-amps are not ideal. At DC, the input transistors draw bias currents I<sub>B+</sub> and I<sub>B−</sub>, and mismatch between the two input halves creates input offset voltage V<sub>OS</sub> and offset current I<sub>OS</sub>. These appear as output errors, especially in high-gain or high-resistance circuits. At large signals or high frequencies, the output can move only so fast; slew rate SR limits it. Supply changes leak to the input as offset, measured by PSRR. Data sheets give all four, plus output swing, input common-mode range and drift. You use them when a sensor front end must hold microvolts, or a video buffer must swing volts quickly.
prereq: You need: CMRR from 5.2, the four op-amp stages from 5.5, and gain-bandwidth product from Unit 3.

sections.h3: Input offset voltage and bias current

blocks.text: Input offset voltage V<sub>OS</sub> is the differential DC voltage you must apply between the inputs to make V<sub>out</sub> = 0. An ideal op-amp needs 0 V. A real one needs a few microvolts to a few millivolts because the input pair and load are not perfectly matched. The sign can be positive or negative. In a unity-gain buffer the output offset equals V<sub>OS</sub>. In a non-inverting amplifier the output error is V<sub>OS</sub>(1 + R<sub>f</sub>/R<sub>i</sub>).

Bias currents I<sub>B+</sub> and I<sub>B−</sub> are the DC currents that flow into the non-inverting and inverting inputs. Their average is the input bias current I<sub>B</sub>. Their mismatch is the input offset current I<sub>OS</sub>. If a resistor R sits at an input, the bias current makes a voltage I<sub>B</sub>R that adds like an offset. For a buffer with source resistance R<sub>s</sub>, the output error from the non-inverting input is I<sub>B+</sub>R<sub>s</sub>. Use equal DC resistances on both inputs to cancel the average I<sub>B</sub>, but I<sub>OS</sub> still causes an error.

blocks.where: I<sub>B+</sub> and I<sub>B−</sub> are the DC currents into the non-inverting and inverting inputs.

blocks.text: V<sub>OS</sub> and I<sub>B</sub> drift with temperature. Data sheets give drift in µV/°C and nA/°C. In a DC sensor front end these errors set the smallest signal you can resolve. Chopper or auto-zero amplifiers reduce them, at the cost of chopping noise and bandwidth.

Slew rate SR is the maximum rate of change of the output: SR = max |dV<sub>out</sub>/dt|. It is a large-signal limit. A small sine wave may pass with good bandwidth, but a large step can still be limited. In a two-stage op-amp the input pair steers the tail current I<sub>5</sub> into the compensation capacitor C<sub>c</sub>, so SR = I<sub>5</sub>/C<sub>c</sub>. The current charging C<sub>c</sub> is I<sub>5</sub> when the input is overdriven.

blocks.where: I<sub>5</sub> is the tail current, C<sub>c</sub> is the compensation capacitor, and V<sub>peak</sub> is the peak sine-wave output voltage.

blocks.text: For a step of size ΔV, the slewing time is t = ΔV/SR. For a sine wave V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>peak</sub> sin(2πft), the maximum slope is 2π f V<sub>peak</sub>. To avoid slew limiting, 2π f V<sub>peak</sub> ≤ SR. The full-power bandwidth is therefore FPBW = SR/(2π V<sub>peak</sub>). Use peak, not peak-to-peak. A 0.5 V/µs op-amp with 2 V peak gives 39.8 kHz.

The input transistor transition frequency fT rises with gm, the input-pair transconductance. Raising I5 to improve SR also raises gm and can hurt stability. Source degeneration lowers the input-pair gm, so for the same gm you can run a larger tail current I5. With the same Cc, SR = I5/Cc then rises. The cost is lower input-stage gain and lower fT. The choice of Cc is part of compensation, covered in 5.7.

sections.h3: PSRR, swing, common-mode range and drift

blocks.text: PSRR measures how much a supply change appears as an input offset. In linear form, PSRR = ΔVOS/ΔVsupply, often in µV/V. In dB, PSRRdB = 20 log10 |Ad/Asupply| = −20 log10 |ΔVOS/ΔVsupply|. Put the ratio in V/V inside the log. Example: PSRR = 100 µV/V = 1 × 10−4 V/V, so PSRRdB = −20 log10(1 × 10−4) = 80 dB. A positive linear PSRR means a positive supply step shifts VOS positive. Data sheets usually quote the magnitude; the dB form is positive for good rejection. PSRR is usually specified separately for +VS and −VS changes. PSRR falls with frequency, so a 1 MHz ripple may pass more easily than DC. CMRR is different: it is about common-mode input, defined in 5.2.

blocks.where: A<sub>d</sub> is the differential gain, A<sub>supply</sub> is the gain from supply to output, and ΔV<sub>supply</sub> is a supply change. Put the ratio in V/V inside the log.

blocks.text: Output swing is the largest V<sub>out</sub> before clipping, given as V<sub>OH</sub> and V<sub>OL</sub> relative to the rails. Input common-mode range is the set of input voltages over which the input pair stays biased; outside it, gain falls and the output may reverse phase. Temperature drift changes V<sub>OS</sub> and I<sub>B</sub>; data sheets give µV/°C and nA/°C. These limits often decide whether you need a rail-to-rail op-amp.

figure.caption: Mismatch in the input pair creates V<sub>OS</sub> and I<sub>OS</sub>; supply changes appear as input offset through PSRR; the compensation capacitor sets the slew-rate limit. All three add to output error or slow the output down; output swing and input common-mode range are separate limits set by the rails and the input stage.

spec.title: Non-ideal op-amp error sources
spec.aria: Block diagram: input mismatch creates Vos and IOS, supply changes create PSRR error, and the compensation capacitor limits slew rate; all three affect the output error and limits.

examples.question: An op-amp has SR = 0.5 V/µs and C<sub>c</sub> = 30 pF. It is used as a unity-gain buffer with a 2 V step. Find the slewing time to 2 V, the full-power bandwidth for a 2 V peak sine wave, and the current charging C<sub>c</sub>.
steps: Convert the slew rate: 0.5 V/µs = 0.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> V/s.
Slewing time: t = ΔV/SR = 2 V / (0.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> V/s) = 4 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s = 4 µs.
Full-power bandwidth: FPBW = SR/(2π V<sub>peak</sub>) = (0.5 × 10<sup>6</sup>) / (2π × 2) = 3.979 × 10<sup>4</sup> Hz = 39.8 kHz.
Charging current: I = C<sub>c</sub> × SR = 30 × 10<sup>−12</sup> F × 0.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> V/s = 15 × 10<sup>−6</sup> A = 15 µA. This current is I<sub>5</sub>.
examples.answer: The slewing time is 4 µs, the full-power bandwidth is 39.8 kHz, and the current charging C<sub>c</sub> is 15 µA.
examples.check:
sr = 0.5e6
cc = 30e-12
dv = 2.0
vp = 2.0
t = dv / sr
f = sr / (2 * 3.141592653589793 * vp)
i = cc * sr
print(round(t * 1e6, 3))
print(round(f / 1e3, 1))
print(round(i * 1e6, 3))

traps: Mixing V/µs with V/s in t = ΔV/SR gives an answer that is wrong by a factor of 10<sup>6</sup>.
Using peak-to-peak voltage in FPBW = SR/(2π V<sub>peak</sub>); the formula needs peak voltage.
Confusing PSRR with CMRR: PSRR is supply-to-input, CMRR is common-mode input to output.
Treating I<sub>OS</sub> as the average bias current; I<sub>OS</sub> is the mismatch |I<sub>B+</sub> − I<sub>B−</sub>|.
Confusing output swing with input common-mode range: one limits V<sub>out</sub>, the other limits the input bias point.

quiz.a: V<sub>OS</sub> is the differential DC input voltage required to make the output voltage zero.

quiz.q: Write the slew-rate formula for a two-stage op-amp and define its terms.
quiz.a: SR = I<sub>5</sub>/C<sub>c</sub>, where I<sub>5</sub> is the tail current of the input stage and C<sub>c</sub> is the compensation capacitor.

quiz.q: Why does input offset current matter even when the average bias current is cancelled?
quiz.a: Equal DC resistances cancel the average I<sub>B</sub>, but the mismatch I<sub>OS</sub> still flows through those resistances and creates an offset voltage.

quiz.q: An op-amp has I<sub>B+</sub> = 80 nA and I<sub>B−</sub> = 60 nA. Find I<sub>B</sub> and I<sub>OS</sub>.
An op-amp has SR = 1 V/µs. Find the full-power bandwidth for a 3 V peak sine wave.
A unity-gain buffer has a 1 MΩ source resistance, V<sub>OS</sub> = 2 mV and I<sub>B</sub> = 50 nA. Which error dominates?
quiz.a: The bias-current error is I<sub>B</sub>R<sub>s</sub> = 50 nA × 1 MΩ = 50 mV. This is much larger than 2 mV, so bias current dominates.

quiz.q: Why does PSRR usually fall as frequency increases?
quiz.a: Supply ripple couples through device capacitances, and the op-amp loop gain falls with frequency. Both make the supply-to-output path stronger relative to the differential gain, so rejection worsens.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, precision op-amps use auto-zero or chopper stabilization to cut V<sub>OS</sub> and drift to microvolts, and current-feedback or decompensated op-amps trade slew rate against stability. High-speed data links and GaN gate drivers care about slew rate and PSRR at megahertz, where datasheet curves matter more than a single number. Search for chopper-stabilized op-amp, PSRR versus frequency, and slew-rate enhancement.
